strengths: First rigorous convergence analysis of SNGD and SPRING algorithms, filling a significant theoretical gap
Novel and elegant connection to randomized Kaczmarz methods provides genuine new insight into algorithm structure
Clean, well-proven results for linear least-squares with clear convergence rate advantages over SGD (Theorem 1)
Rigorous mathematical treatment with detailed proofs and sound technical development throughout
Well-written paper with clear problem formulation, precise statements of contributions, and logical progression
Identification of when regularization is necessary for LLQ (Proposition 3) provides new understanding
weaknesses: Severe gap between motivation (non-convex neural networks in NNWs/PINNs) and analysis (linear models with convex losses) undermines practical relevance
Strong Assumption 2 for LLQ (range(HJ) ⊆ range(J)) acknowledged as unlikely in practice, severely limiting applicability
SPRING analysis for LLQ incomplete—only Conjecture 7 provided despite numerical evidence of dramatic acceleration (Figure 1), a critical gap
Theory for LLS heavily relies on applying existing Kaczmarz analyses; main novelty is recognizing equivalence rather than new proof techniques
Limited experimental validation: only synthetic Gaussian problems tested, no experiments on actual NNW or PINN benchmarks
Convergence rates depend on unknown problem-specific quantities (α, κ values); no practical guidance for setting regularization λ beyond necessity
Strong consistency assumption (Jθ* = b for LLS) required but not universal; inconsistent systems not addressed
Restrictive assumptions for Corollary 5 (Gaussian data, polynomial spectral decay) reduce practical applicability

strengths: Novel sketch-and-project perspective on SNG that productively addresses gap in existing theory regarding small-sample behavior where k ≪ n
Lemma 4.1 elegantly handles coupled gradient-preconditioner challenge via SVS expectation formulas, enabling analysis without decoupling

Valuable theoretical insight that SNG exploits spectral decay in J superlinearly (scaling as α), explaining practical effectiveness compared to SGD's linear scaling, with strong empirical validation (Figure 4)
Empirically demonstrates SVS-SNG is superior theoretical proxy to two-mini-batch methods at capturing realistic single-mini-batch algorithm behavior (Figures 2, 6)
Theorem 6.1 provides elegant explanation of SPRING algorithm structure as accelerated sketch-and-project, clarifying previously mysterious algorithm
Technically sound proofs with comprehensive treatment; rigorous convergence analysis for LLQ setting
Clear presentation, effective motivation for scientific ML applications (NNWs, PINNs), and well-organized appendices
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: SVS is impractical to implement efficiently; paper acknowledges this but provides no theoretical guarantees that uniform sampling (used in practice) approximates SVS behavior, limiting practical relevance

Incomplete characterization of key quantity γ: appears crucially in Theorem 5.1 convergence rates but Proposition 5.3 provides only preliminary bounds (γ=1 only at extremes); thorough analysis deferred to future work, creating significant gap

Incomplete main results: Theorem 6.1 (SPRING) proven only for linear least-squares, with Conjecture 6.2 for LLQ unproven; convergence rate analysis (Theorem 5.1) restricted to LLQ model problem rather than general parametric optimization

Limited experimental validation: all experiments on synthetic LLQ problems with controlled Gaussian spectra; no validation on actual applications (NNWs, PINNs) that motivate the work, limiting evidence of practical utility
Restrictive assumptions: condition on ‖r‖² in Theorem 4.2 only verified for LLQ; extension to infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces needed for PINNs but deferred
Methodological concern: core SVS tool is not novel; main novelty is application to SNG, and once SVS connection established, some results follow mechanically from existing sketch-and-project theory
No theoretical path to practical algorithm: paper suggests negative correlation in mini-batches as future direction but provides no concrete proposals or guarantees
